basis: Hazard intensity layers in physical units by return period (E169). Each layer is a published dataset read as it is, or derived from a registered event set by a stated method; samples are stored per layer version in hazard_intensity_samples.

jrc_river_flood.name: JRC global river-flood maps
jrc_river_flood.source: JRC / Copernicus EMS global river flood hazard maps (CEMS-GLOFAS flood_hazard), LISFLOOD-FP
jrc_river_flood.dry_basis: depths of 0.05 m or less are raster noise and read as dry (ml.scoring.flood_jrc.DEPTH_MIN_M)
jrc_river_flood.coverage: river flooding only, global land; pluvial and coastal flooding are other channels
jrc_river_flood.licence_status: to verify against the JRC data catalogue entry before customer-facing use

storm_v4_wind.name: STORM tropical-cyclone wind maps
storm_v4_wind.source: derived from the event set storm_v4: per synthetic year, the highest wind at the point
storm_v4_wind.wind_field: modified Rankine vortex as ml.scoring.storm_physics (the calibrated storm channel)
storm_v4_wind.coverage: the six STORM basins (EP, NA, NI, SI, SP, WP)
storm_v4_wind.metric_basis: STORM's generator states its wind as 'Vmax10: 10-minute mean maximum sustained wind speed of the TC (m/s)' (github.com/NBloemendaal/STORM, SAMPLE_TC_PRESSURE.py, line 37)
storm_v4_wind.domain_note: STORM's basins run 'with lat boundaries set at 60 N/S' (SELECT_BASIN.py, line 92) with no extratropical transition, and its tracks reach Europe more often than observed ones (Madrid: 15% of simulated years within 400 km against 3 of 46 observed seasons, 2026-10-06): a loss is computed only where an adopted cyclone curve covers the country

max_sustained_wind_1min.decided: the product owner's decision of 2026-10-20: undo STORM's own step, so the 1-minute winds the cyclone curves are stated in are the ones STORM started from
max_sustained_wind_1min.basis: STORM turned the warning centres' 1-minute winds into its 10-minute ones: 'These wind speeds are multiplied by a factor of 0.88 to convert them to U10' (Bloemendaal et al. 2020, Methods, Input datasets, citing Harper, Kepert & Ginger's guidelines, WMO 2008); dividing by 0.88 restores that 1-minute basis. CLIMADA, the code the Eberenz curves were calibrated with, does the same for STORM: 'STORM_1MIN_WIND_FACTOR = 0.88' and 'tracks_df["wind"] /= STORM_1MIN_WIND_FACTOR'. The final WMO guidelines (WMO/TD-No. 1555, section 1.5) recommend 0.93 for at-sea storm maxima and say this 'is about 5% higher than the "traditional" value of 0.88, which is seen to be more appropriate to an off-land exposure' (Table 1.2: at-sea 0.93, off-sea 0.90, off-land 0.87, in-land 0.84).

Guidelines for converting between various wind averaging periods in tropical cyclone conditions (WMO/TD-No. 1555)
sources.authors: Harper, B. A., Kepert, J. D. and Ginger, J. D.
sources.copy: the lead author's copy (systemsengineeringaustralia.com.au, Systems Engineering Australia), dated 27-Aug-2010, cover 'WMO/TD-No. 1555'; WMO's library sits behind a human check

jrc_flood_30m.name: 30 m flood refinement
jrc_flood_30m.source: the JRC river-flood maps (jrc_river_flood) re-spread over the Copernicus DEM GLO-30 Public surface
jrc_flood_30m.method: the JRC 1-in-100-year depth (90 m) re-spread over the Copernicus GLO-30 surface (30 m): in each wet 90 m pixel the water surface is the mean 30 m elevation of its land sub-pixels plus the mapped depth; a 30 m sub-pixel is wet where that surface stands more than 0.05 m above it. Water never spreads outside the pixels the JRC maps flood
jrc_flood_30m.licence_status: GLO-30: to verify before customer-facing use (data/reference/supply_datasets.json)

test.rule: the refinement is used only when, on the same nodes, BOTH its pooled Spearman rank correlation with the observed share AND its pooled AUC (observed share > 2%) are higher than the 90 m maps'; otherwise the 90 m maps stay and the result is recorded

building_scale_test.rule: the refinement is better at building scale only when the 5th percentile of the resampled difference in pooled CSI (30 m minus 90 m) is above zero; when the 95th percentile is below zero it is worse; otherwise the test cannot tell them apart

decision.basis: neither test could tell the 30 m layer from the 90 m maps: node scale ρ +0.0015 and AUC +0.0009 inside sampling noise; building scale CSI 0.223 vs 0.221 with a 90% interval of −0.005 to +0.007. Adopting would change loss figures and fetch ~5 GB more with no evidence of a gain
decision.revisit_when: a test at building scale against observed losses or a finer observed extent shows a gain beyond the registered noise margin

aqueduct_river_flood.name: WRI Aqueduct flood projections
aqueduct_river_flood.source: WRI Aqueduct Floods hazard maps v2.0, riverine inundation (GLOFRIS: PCR-GLOBWB 2 at 5′, downscaled to 30″ by volume spreading)
aqueduct_river_flood.citation: Ward, P.J., H.C. Winsemius, S. Kuzma, et al. 2020. 'Aqueduct Floods Methodology.' Technical Note. Washington, D.C.: World Resources Institute
aqueduct_river_flood.resolution_basis: 'regridded to 30 × 30 arc seconds (30″ × 30″)—about 1 km × 1 km at the equator' (Ward et al. 2020, section 2)
aqueduct_river_flood.dry_basis: Aqueduct counts a cell as impacted 'when water levels exceed 0 m' (Ward et al. 2020, section 2); no-data (−9999) is dry
aqueduct_river_flood.reads_as: the 30″ pixel holding the asset, as Aqueduct reads urban damage 'from the occurring water depth in that grid cell' (section 2): share 1 when the pixel is wet, its depth as the mean

present.covers: 1960–1999, forced by observed weather (EU-WATCH) — 'assumed as the present-day values' (appendix A.1.1)

aqueduct_river_flood.future_method: 'changes in future flood volumes were calculated, for all GCMs, from differences between the values in future (RCP and GCM combination) and historical (GCM) conditions … We then imposed the difference to the present-day run forced with the EUWATCH dataset' (appendix A.1.1)
aqueduct_river_flood.flood_protection: 'The hazard layers have been simulated without considering the presence of flood protection' (section 3) — as jrc_river_flood
aqueduct_river_flood.licence_status: verified: WRI's catalogue record for the dataset (datasets.wri.org API, package aqueduct-floods-hazard-maps) states license_id 'cc-by'; attribution: the citation above (2026-10-07)

use.role: projected runs only; today's official flood figure stays jrc_river_flood
use.compared_with: its own present-day map only — a projected figure is never subtracted from or set against a jrc_river_flood figure
use.range: central: the middle (median) of the five models; low: the lowest model's curve-low figure; high: the highest model's curve-high figure — the spread of the curve and of the models together

timeline.rule: a pathway-year reads the two maps whose warming brackets its own — the present day or any pathway's map — the water depth blended by how far its warming lies between theirs, then the damage curve applied; warmer than every map, a named gap
timeline.present_made_from: observations — the present-day run is 'forced with the EUWATCH dataset' (appendix A.1.1), measured on the observed record
timeline.maps_basis: same 2100 radiative forcing: RCP4.5 ↔ SSP2-4.5, RCP8.5 ↔ SSP5-8.5; each map is climate-model output, measured on the assessed series of the SSP with its forcing

agreement_at_assets.basis: JRC wet: the location's H3 res-8 cell has a flooded share; Aqueduct wet: its 30″ pixel is wet

jrc_river_flood_europe.name: JRC European river-flood maps
jrc_river_flood_europe.source: JRC / Copernicus EMS river flood hazard maps for Europe and the Mediterranean Basin region (CEMS-EFAS flood_hazard): LISFLOOD river flow, LISFLOOD-FP inundation
jrc_river_flood_europe.citation: Baugh, C., Colonese, J., D'Angelo, C., Dottori, F., Neal, J., Prudhomme, C., Salamon, P. (2024): An updated dataset of global and European flood hazard maps. Manuscript under preparation (README A01)
jrc_river_flood_europe.dry_basis: read as the global JRC maps are (jrc_river_flood): no-data (−9999) is dry, depths of 0.05 m or less are raster noise; permanent water bodies (the README's mask, value 1) are neither land nor flooded
jrc_river_flood_europe.caution: the publisher's spurious-depth mask: 'areas where depths >10m are predicted in small channels (<3,000km^2) for the 10-year return period, plus a 2km buffer … Users should exercise caution when using the depth values in these areas' (README F02) — a location whose cell touches it carries that caution with its figure; the figure is not dropped
jrc_river_flood_europe.coverage: river flooding only; European extended domain (README D01), land only (D03); the maps publish no domain outline, so the layer serves only assets whose stated country is in coverage_countries
jrc_river_flood_europe.coverage_countries: UN M49 Europe (150) less Russia, Belarus and Ukraine — the countries the JRC protection map covers
jrc_river_flood_europe.licence: CC BY 4.0 — 'Any copyright and/or sui generis right on the dataset is licensed under the Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 International (CC BY 4.0) licence … Reuse is allowed provided appropriate credit is given and any changes are indicated' (copyright.txt held beside the data); README A02: 'no restrictions, free and open Copernicus product'
jrc_river_flood_europe.adoption: in use inside coverage_countries since 2026-10-16: the registered check did not refuse it (product owner's decision, 2026-10-16)

test.rule: the European maps replace the global maps inside coverage_countries unless they rank the observed floods worse: refused when the 95th percentile of the paired-bootstrap difference (European − global; 2,000 resamples of the nodes, seed 7) is below zero for the rank correlation OR for the AUC (observed share > 2%)

aqueduct_coastal_flood.name: WRI Aqueduct coastal flood maps
aqueduct_coastal_flood.source: WRI Aqueduct Floods hazard maps v2.0, coastal inundation: extreme sea levels (tide and storm surge) from the Global Tide and Surge Reanalysis enriched with IBTrACS cyclone tracks, spread over the MERIT terrain at 30″ by a GIS inundation routine
aqueduct_coastal_flood.citation: Ward, P.J., H.C. Winsemius, S. Kuzma, et al. 2020. 'Aqueduct Floods Methodology.' Technical Note. Washington, D.C.: World Resources Institute
aqueduct_coastal_flood.method_basis: 'We used all tracks over the period 1979–2014, converted these into wind and pressure fields, and simulated water levels accordingly. We combined the time series of GTSR and the cyclone track simulations by using the highest value found within the time series and established extreme values using a Gumbel extreme value distribution fit on the annual extremes. To translate near-shore tide and surge levels to overland inundation, we applied a GIS-based inundation routine … The routine inundates areas that are hydraulically connected to the sea at a given extreme sea level' (Ward et al. 2020, appendix A.1.3)
aqueduct_coastal_flood.resolution_basis: 'The model uses the Multi-Error-Removed Improved-Terrain (MERIT) DEM (Yamazaki et al. 2017) at a 30″ × 30″ resolution as underlying topography' (Ward et al. 2020, appendix A.1.3)

files.dictionary: WRI's data dictionary (_Aqueduct_Floods_Data_Dictionary.xlsx, read 2026-10-23): projection '0' = '95th percentile (default)', '0_perc_05' = '5th percentile', '0_perc_50' = '50th percentile'; 'wtsub' = 'Subsidence included'

aqueduct_coastal_flood.dry_basis: Aqueduct counts a cell as impacted 'when water levels exceed 0 m' (Ward et al. 2020, section 2): a depth of 0 m is dry

no_data.basis: 'The value of -9999 is used as NoData' (WRI's catalogue record for the maps, datasets.wri.org, read 2026-10-23); on the coastal maps no-data is the sea and land beyond the maps' reach (read 2026-10-23: open North Sea −9999, Dutch coastal land 0 m or a depth) — a location there is outside the map, with no value, never a zero

aqueduct_coastal_flood.reads_as: the 30″ pixel holding the asset, as Aqueduct reads urban damage 'from the occurring water depth in that grid cell' (section 2): share 1 when the pixel is wet, its depth as the mean

present.covers: extreme sea levels of 1979–2014 (the GTSR reanalysis and IBTrACS cyclone tracks, appendix A.1.3), today's sea level

aqueduct_coastal_flood.members_basis: sea-level rise from RISES-AM (Jevrejeva et al. 2014): 'We chose the 50 percent projection for this project and have also established inundation estimates using the 5th and 95th percentiles' (Ward et al. 2020, appendix A.1.3); a member is the map at that percentile

subsidence.basis: the maps that include it ('wtsub' — 'Subsidence included', the data dictionary): 'Land subsidence—the lowering of the land level—is an important variable used for calculating future flood risk. In many coastal areas, groundwater extraction is the dominant cause of human-induced land subsidence' (Ward et al. 2020, section 3); a map placed on the warming timeline carries its year's subsidence with it — the product owner's choice of 2026-10-23

aqueduct_coastal_flood.flood_protection: 'The hazard layers have been simulated without considering the presence of flood protection' (section 3); no published coastal protection standard is held, so every coastal figure is the undefended one
aqueduct_coastal_flood.coverage: coastal flooding (tide and storm surge, with sea-level rise and subsidence in the future maps), global coasts. River flooding is the flood peril's: 'simply adding damage estimates for riverine and coastal together could result in double-counting; on the other, some areas may suffer increased hazard due to compound effects' (Ward et al. 2020, section 8) — the two are shown side by side, never added
aqueduct_coastal_flood.licence_status: verified: WRI's catalogue record for the dataset (datasets.wri.org API, package aqueduct-floods-hazard-maps) states license_id 'cc-by'; attribution: the citation above — one package for the riverine and coastal maps (2026-10-07; re-read 2026-10-23)

use.role: today's coastal flood figure (its present-day map) and projected runs (its pathway maps)
use.range: central: the 50th percentile of sea-level rise; low: the 5th percentile's curve-low figure; high: the 95th percentile's curve-high figure — the spread of sea-level rise and of the curve together

timeline.rule: a pathway-year reads the two maps whose warming brackets its own — the present day or any pathway's map — the water depth blended by how far its warming lies between theirs, then the damage curve applied; warmer than every map, a named gap
timeline.present_made_from: observations — extreme sea levels from the GTSR reanalysis and IBTrACS best tracks of 1979–2014 (appendix A.1.3), measured on the observed record
timeline.maps_basis: same 2100 radiative forcing: RCP4.5 ↔ SSP2-4.5, RCP8.5 ↔ SSP5-8.5; each map is climate-model output, measured on the assessed series of the SSP with its forcing
timeline.periods_basis: the source's years: 'In Aqueduct Floods, flood risk is calculated for 2010, 2030, 2050, and 2080' (Ward et al. 2020, section 2) — a coastal map holds the sea level of its year, measured on the year's assessed 20-year level

storm_cc_wind.name: STORM future tropical-cyclone wind maps
storm_cc_wind.source: derived from the event set storm_cc (STORM Climate Change synthetic tracks): per climate model and synthetic year, the highest wind at the point — the method of storm_v4_wind
storm_cc_wind.wind_field: modified Rankine vortex as ml.scoring.storm_physics (the calibrated storm channel)
storm_cc_wind.coverage: the six STORM basins (EP, NA, NI, SI, SP, WP)
storm_cc_wind.licence_status: verified: the dataset record (figshare API, article 14237678) states licence 'CC0' (2026-10-23)
storm_cc_wind.metric_basis: the record's README: entry 9 'Maximum wind speed' in m/s, the columns 'copied from Bloemendaal et al 2020' — the measure of storm_v4_wind (STORM's 'Vmax10: 10-minute mean maximum sustained wind speed')
storm_cc_wind.domain_note: STORM's basins run 'with lat boundaries set at 60 N/S' (SELECT_BASIN.py, line 92) with no extratropical transition, and its tracks reach Europe more often than observed ones (Madrid: 15% of simulated years within 400 km against 3 of 46 observed seasons, 2026-10-06): a loss is computed only where an adopted cyclone curve covers the country

max_sustained_wind_1min.decided: the product owner's decision of 2026-10-20 for STORM's winds (storm_v4_wind), which this set shares: the same generator, its tracks' winds in the same measure ('Maximum wind speed m/s', the columns 'copied from Bloemendaal et al 2020', the record's README)
max_sustained_wind_1min.basis: STORM turned the warning centres' 1-minute winds into its 10-minute ones: 'These wind speeds are multiplied by a factor of 0.88 to convert them to U10' (Bloemendaal et al. 2020, Methods, Input datasets, citing Harper, Kepert & Ginger's guidelines, WMO 2008); dividing by 0.88 restores that 1-minute basis. CLIMADA, the code the Eberenz curves were calibrated with, does the same for STORM: 'STORM_1MIN_WIND_FACTOR = 0.88' and 'tracks_df["wind"] /= STORM_1MIN_WIND_FACTOR'. The final WMO guidelines (WMO/TD-No. 1555, section 1.5) recommend 0.93 for at-sea storm maxima and say this 'is about 5% higher than the "traditional" value of 0.88, which is seen to be more appropriate to an off-land exposure' (Table 1.2: at-sea 0.93, off-sea 0.90, off-land 0.87, in-land 0.84).

Guidelines for converting between various wind averaging periods in tropical cyclone conditions (WMO/TD-No. 1555)
sources.authors: Harper, B. A., Kepert, J. D. and Ginger, J. D.
sources.copy: the lead author's copy (systemsengineeringaustralia.com.au, Systems Engineering Australia), dated 27-Aug-2010, cover 'WMO/TD-No. 1555'; WMO's library sits behind a human check

present.covers: STORM's present climate: 10,000 years generated from IBTrACS 1980–2018

use.role: projected runs only; today's tropical-cyclone figure stays storm_v4_wind
use.compared_with: the same generator's present climate (storm_v4_wind) only
use.range: central: the median of the four models — the mean of the two middle models' figures, ranked by expected yearly loss; low: the lowest model's curve-low figure; high: the highest model's curve-high figure

timeline.rule: a pathway-year reads the two maps whose warming brackets its own — the present climate or the future set — the wind at each return period blended by how far its warming lies between theirs, then the damage curve applied; warmer than every map, a named gap
timeline.present_made_from: observations — STORM's input is drawn 'from the global historical dataset IBTrACS for the time period 1980–2018 (38 years of data)' (Bloemendaal et al. 2020, Scientific Data 7, 40), measured on the observed record
timeline.maps_basis: the record: 'The dataset is generated by extracting the climate change signal from each of the four general circulation models listed below, and adding this signal to the historical data from IBTrACS … and resembles future-climate (2015-2050; RCP8.5/SSP5) conditions' (figshare article 14237678, read 2026-10-23)

jrc_flood_protection_europe.name: JRC flood-protection map
jrc_flood_protection_europe.source: JRC PESETA IV floods collection — 'map of estimated flood defence standards in Europe … Cell values indicate the estimated return period of design (in years) of local protection structures against river floods' (PESETA IV collection description v3, 3 October 2022)
jrc_flood_protection_europe.citation: Dottori, F., Mentaschi, L., Bianchi, A., Alfieri, L., Feyen, L. (2023): Cost-effective adaptation strategies to rising river flood risk in Europe. Nature Climate Change 13, 196–202 (doi:10.1038/s41558-022-01540-0) — 'Dottori et al. (2022)' in the collection description
jrc_flood_protection_europe.built_from: 'The new dataset combine information on protection design levels with modelled protection standards calculated by Jongman et al. (2014) and Scussolini et al. (2016)' (Dottori et al. 2020, EUR 29955 EN, Annex A1.2)
jrc_flood_protection_europe.reads_as: the 500 m pixel holding the asset's location: its design return period; no-data (−1) or a location off the map is 'protection unknown'
jrc_flood_protection_europe.coverage: 'all countries in geographical Europe bar Russia, Belarus, Ukraine, and countries in the Caucasus (due to lack of information)' (collection description)
jrc_flood_protection_europe.licence: CC BY 4.0 (copyright.txt held beside the data, the same notice as the flood maps')

coastpros_eu.name: COASTPROS-EU coastal protection standards
coastpros_eu.source: COASTPROS-EU: coastal flood protection standards per coastal NUTS2 region of Europe (148 regions, 24 countries), compiled from georeferenced defence data, policy design standards and, where neither was found, the levels modelled by Tiggeloven et al. (2020)
coastpros_eu.citation: De Plaen, J. J.-F. G., Colmenares, M., Koks, E., Scussolini, P. et al. (2025): COASTPROS-EU [dataset], Zenodo, doi:10.5281/zenodo.15024139
coastpros_eu.creators: as the record lists them: De Plaen, Joël J.-F. G.; Colmenares, Maria; Koks, Elco; Scussolini, Paolo; Lena, Reimann; Lincke, Daniel; Kiesel, Joshua; Wolff, Claudia; Tiggeloven, Timothy; Peregrina Gonzalez, Edgar Daniel; Le Cozannet, Goneri; Sayers, Paul
coastpros_eu.reads_basis: the dataset's metadata: 'SUMMARY RETURN PERIOD: Provides the most detailed information collected on the coastal defence for each NUTS2 based on the previous columns. If available, it will list the georeferenced defence standards. If not, it will provide policy guidelines. If not, available we finally resort to the values modelled by Tiggeloven et., al. (2020).' (COASTPROS-EU.xlsx, sheet Metadata; the shapefile's column 'SUMMARY RE')

reading.rule: clean entries only: a single number is the region's design level; a plain range 'a-b' is a range of levels — the defended loss a range, low at the upper level, high at the lower level, with no central figure; a list, a condition or a note is no level (protection unknown); an empty entry is no value (protection unknown)

coastpros_eu.reads_as: the NUTS2 region holding the asset's location (a point in a listed region's polygon, the polygon's edge included); a location in no listed region is off the map — protection unknown
coastpros_eu.coverage: the coasts of 24 European countries (AL, BE, DE, DK, EE, EL, ES, FI, FR, HR, IE, IT, LT, LV, ME, MK, MT, NL, NO, PL, PT, SE, SI, UK — the dataset's own codes)
coastpros_eu.applies_basis: WRI applies protection standards to coastal floods as to river floods: 'FLOPROS is a database of current protection standards for both riverine and coastal floods' and 'The flood protection is added to the risk curve as a vertical line' (Ward et al. 2020, section 6)
coastpros_eu.licence_status: verified: the Zenodo record (API, record 15024139) states license 'cc-by-4.0' (2026-10-23)
